name: Zabban ibn Sayyar
bio: Zabban ibn Sayyar of Fazarah, of the Mazin house, is the Zabban who, according to Lyall, nicknamed al-Hadirah. Lyall introduces his odes with the war of Dahis between the tribes of 'Abs and Dhubyan.
Two of his poems are in the Mufaddaliyat, Odes CII and CIII.

poems.title: Ode CII: Ye Sons of Manulah ! in
poems.author: Zabban ibn Sayyar
poems.note: Lyall's heading: Zabban son of Sayyar, of the house of Mazin.
poems.text:
Ye Sons of Manulah ! in sooth I obeyed your chiefs, hoping that there might be a way to avoid war with friends ;

And the Sons of Umayyah — all of them would be leaders and captains, and the Sons of Kiyah the same, when a matter is debated in council.

Go thy way ! Verily companies of the House of Murrah dwelling in the Hijaz shall surely defend their herds of camels —

Groups of men whom they have settled there in the spacious plain, as though they were princes ruling between Manbij and al-Kathib.

And when I move in reply to a cry for help, there gallops with my weapons a stout mare, short-haired, high in the withers, taking short steps [through sprightliness],

Beautiful of shape, one that gallops hard when I push her on, very speedy when her girth is wet with sweat, an excellent canterer :

I have made her ready against the Sons of al-Laqitah : she carries my spear, and a keen sword, and a small coat of mail,

And a man experienced in distressful cases, who does not flinch when tribes meet tribes in conflict.

poems.title: Ode CIII: Does not their knowledge of Zabban
poems.author: Zabban ibn Sayyar
poems.text:
Does not their knowledge of Zabban suffice to restrain the Sons of al-Laqitah, that they attack him with lampoons, while he sleeps [and gives no heed to them] ?

They go about with the Weak-eyed one, while there is poured forth upon them a tongue keen like the edge of an Indian sword.

Yet in al-Haba'ah there is a slain man lying, in whose hinder part is stuck a writing that should warn the wrong-doer from returning to wrong !

When ye read it, it will bring you guidance out of your error, and well shall it be known when the seals are broken away ;

There where the horses were tethered in the place where your Father lay, a man of sound judgement, hard in his enmity, left it as a gift for you.

And if ye ask about it the riders of Dahis, there is one of the house of Rawahah who knows and can give you tidings.

Sharik son of Malik swore, lighthearted and full of spirit, that when we met in battle, never would he make peace with his foe :

He swore that never willingly would he accept the position of a defeated man. Yea, thou shalt come to that, and thy nose be rubbed in the dust !
